Content that can keep up with the models
As the Anthropic team prepared to launch Claude 3.5 Sonnet in 2024, they needed a documentation platform that could grow with the rapid product adoption and influx of new users.

It immediately paid off, with the new docs experience launching in just three weeks. Tailoring the docs to match Claude's brand was fast, and Mintlify's docs-as-code workflow made updating content significantly easier for developers and collaborators alike.
It was really impressive to see how fast we could ship our docs with Mintlify.

When Mintlify shipped llms.txt support across every site on the platform in 2024, it took a months-old proposal and put thousands of developer tools on it overnight. Anthropic's docs were among the first live, with no implementation work on their end. The two teams then developed llms-full.txt together, and that format was subsequently adopted into the official spec.

Claude Code's documentation receives millions of visitors each month and is run by one person: Sarah Deaton, technical content engineer. She is pushing Mintlify and Anthropic tools to their limit finding ways to automate and augment her work. But one of the toughest parts of the job is knowing whether your documentation is helping users succeed, and how to improve.
Technical Content Engineer at Anthropic

All of this information serves as context for Claude to improve the documentation. The labor of sourcing feedback, identifying valid content gaps, and drafting content is automated. The result is documentation that functions as its own feedback loop rather than a static surface.

Not every signal coming through Claude Code's docs is a documentation problem. Some of it points to friction in the product itself, and now Sarah can take those fixes straight to the source. Feedback that would otherwise sit in a docs backlog reaches the product team directly, so user experience issues get solved rather than explained.

"I'm able to submit a PR to fix the actual product," she explains. "That short-circuits the loop of needing to document around a paper cut. You just fix the issue. Make it so that people don't even need to go to the documentation."

Anthropic moved its docs to Mintlify in 2024 to ship documentation fast without building infrastructure. Today, that decision is paying dividends. It shows up in the feedback loop that lets one writer run the documentation for Claude Code, turning reader signals into merged pull requests and product updates.

CDP's docs ran on a static site generator that made updates slow and wasn't designed to make content available to AI agents. Coinbase needed faster publishing and agent access without assigning engineers to build and maintain a new documentation platform.

Onchain protocols evolve constantly, and every change impacts our docs. Publishing updates with our old setup kept us from moving at the speed we needed, since content freshness directly affects whether a developer's first build works—and whether they decide to continue working with us.

After evaluating several vendors, Coinbase chose Mintlify. Its new CDP developer experience went live just six weeks later, and the value keeps compounding. Before Mintlify, a single documentation update could take more than 20 minutes. Now it takes under 60 seconds, ensuring content is always accurate and aligned with rapidly evolving onchain protocols.

"AI-native docs are essential when you're building with tools like MCP and x402," says Leffew. "Mintlify helps us deliver a developer experience at Coinbase that feels as agentic as the protocols we're shipping."
Since switching to Mintlify, CDP has seen developers arrive directly at the content they need, with 98.3% of sessions starting on a page other than the docs homepage.

Better information architecture and automatic SEO and AEO optimization enable developers to land directly on the exact content they need to succeed. And once they're there, an interactive API playground lets them fire real API calls without leaving the page.
Private previews for beta APIs

In six weeks, Coinbase went from a static documentation site to knowledge infrastructure that ships updates in seconds, answers developers on the spot, and hands its content to agents in the format they expect. And the team is far from finished.

"We recently launched a private preview doc site that's password protected via Mintlify," shares Leffew. "This is how we share beta APIs with select customers before public release, and so far it's been a big success."

argues that "self-updating documentation is an infinite market," based on the perspective that the primary readers of documentation are shifting from humans to AI agents.

What was interesting is that, despite documentation being a rather mundane subject, the numbers are moving significantly. In this article, I will organize where those numbers come from, how they are counted, and how far we can interpret them.
I will also cover how we should think about documentation that is intended to be read by machines.

I should state this upfront: Mr. Foster is an employee of Mintlify, which provides a documentation infrastructure.
